summary.text: A 49-year-old woman presented with significant dissatisfaction with the aesthetics of an anterior tooth with gingival recession, having had orthodontic treatment seven years earlier. Examination of tooth 23 showed a 12 mm deep and 6 mm wide recession, Miller Class III, 1 mm of keratinized tissue, bleeding on probing, slight calculus, grade III mobility and extensive periapical and lateral radiolucency.

An endodontist found a negative cold test and indicated endodontic treatment. The tooth was diagnosed as a primary endodontic lesion with secondary periodontal involvement and given a poor to guarded prognosis due to severe periodontal attachment loss. After discussing options, the patient decided to keep the tooth, and the lesion was later retrospectively classified as a primary endodontic lesion after healing following root canal therapy.

Treatment began with oral hygiene instructions, scaling and root planing and a temporary splint, then root canal therapy. Four months later probing depths were within 3 mm and radiolucency had decreased slightly. Root coverage was done with a laterally positioned flap and subepithelial connective tissue graft, followed by ibuprofen, chlorhexidine rinse and postoperative instructions, with sutures removed after two weeks and recall visits.

Healing was uneventful. At 6 months the canine showed 1 mm recession, root coverage of 91.7% and a gain of attachment of 13 mm, with a moderate decrease in radiolucency. At 2 years recession was 2.5 mm with a slight lateral radiolucency, and at 18 years the radiograph showed complete resolution of the lesion, with successful radiographic and clinical results over 18 years.
